title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's independent Senate campaigns in Nebraska have shown Democrats a different way to compete in deep-red states: step back from the party label, elevate locally credible candidates, and make the race about class, corruption, and independence rather than national partisan identity.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: For years, Democratic strategy in deep-red states has often followed the same frustrating pattern: recruit a Democrat, nationalize the race around Republican extremism, raise money from angry national donors, and then lose by margins that confirm the state was never truly competitive. Dan Osborn's campaigns in Nebraska have challenged that model. He has not made Nebraska blue, and he has not solved the Democratic Party's problems in rural America. But he has shown that the traditional party label is sometimes the obstacle, not the vehicle.

Osborn's importance comes from the fact that he is not running as a Democrat. He is running as an independent, leaning into a working-class, anti-establishment identity that fits Nebraska better than a standard national Democratic brand. In a state where the Democratic label carries heavy baggage, his campaigns have tested a different theory: the path to competitiveness may require Democrats to support candidates who do not look, sound, or campaign like Democrats at all.

The 2024 Nebraska Senate race was the proof of concept. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but he turned what should have been a safely Republican race into a surprisingly close contest. He ran far ahead of the Democratic presidential baseline in the state, showing that there was a pool of voters willing to consider a non-Republican candidate if that candidate was not packaged as a national Democrat.

That result mattered because it separated ideological persuasion from partisan branding. A voter can be deeply Republican in presidential politics while still being open to a labor-backed independent who talks about wages, corporations, political corruption, and working people. Osborn's appeal is not that he converts Nebraska into a Democratic state. It is that he gives anti-establishment, economically populist voters permission to oppose a Republican incumbent without feeling like they are joining the Democratic coalition.

That is why his 2026 campaign against Pete Ricketts is so important. Ricketts is not merely another Republican incumbent. He is a wealthy former governor, a major figure in Nebraska Republican politics, and exactly the kind of opponent Osborn's message is designed to run against. The contrast is simple: mechanic and union leader versus billionaire politician. In a normal Democratic campaign, that message might be drowned out by national culture-war branding. In an independent campaign, it becomes the center of the race.

Nebraska Democrats appear to have learned from 2024. Rather than insist on running a conventional Democratic nominee in 2026, the party's strategy has moved toward clearing space for Osborn. Cindy Burbank winning the Democratic primary while planning to withdraw in favor of Osborn is unusual, but it reflects the logic of the race. If the goal is to defeat Ricketts, a Democrat on the ballot could split the anti-Ricketts vote or make the race easier to nationalize. Osborn needs a one-on-one contest, not a three-way race that lets Republicans frame him as a Democrat in disguise.

The broader lesson for Democrats is uncomfortable but useful. In some deep-red states, the party may be too weak to win under its own name but still strong enough to help build an anti-Republican coalition. That means the best Democratic strategy may not always be to nominate the strongest Democrat. Sometimes it may be to avoid crowding the lane, support an independent indirectly, and let the campaign develop its own identity.

This does not mean Democrats can simply copy and paste the Osborn model everywhere. Nebraska has a specific political culture, a history of independent-minded politics, and a candidate with a biography that fits the state. Osborn is a Navy veteran, National Guardsman, mechanic, and union leader. That combination gives him credibility that a generic outsider candidate would not automatically have. The model depends on the candidate being believable, not just independent on paper.

It also requires restraint from national Democrats. If Osborn is seen as a Democratic project, the strategy weakens. His strength comes from distance: distance from Washington, distance from party leadership, and distance from the usual partisan language. Democrats can benefit from his campaign, but they cannot smother it. The more the race looks like Nebraska versus the political class, the better it is for Osborn. The more it looks like Chuck Schumer versus Pete Ricketts, the better it is for Republicans.

The risk is that even a strong independent campaign may still fall short. Nebraska remains a deeply Republican state, and Ricketts begins with major structural advantages. Republican voters may return home by Election Day, national Republican groups may spend heavily to define Osborn, and the absence of a party label does not erase polarization. Osborn's path is real, but narrow.

Still, the fact that the race is even worth discussing is the point. Osborn has redefined what Democratic-aligned strategy can look like in the deep red. He has shown that the question is not always how Democrats can make voters like the Democratic Party. Sometimes the better question is how anti-Republican forces can build a candidate and message that fit the state they are trying to win.

For Senate control, that matters. Democrats do not have many obvious pickup opportunities, and the Senate map often forces them to compete on Republican terrain. If they want to expand the battlefield, they may need more candidates who can scramble the usual partisan assumptions. Osborn's campaign is not a guaranteed win. But it is a serious experiment in how to compete where the Democratic brand alone is not enough.

In that sense, Dan Osborn's 2026 campaign is bigger than Nebraska. It is a test of whether Democrats can be strategically flexible in places where their party label has become a ceiling. If Osborn comes close again, the lesson will be that deep-red states are not impossible, but they require a different kind of politics. If he wins, it could become one of the most important Senate strategy shifts of the decade.

title: Paths for Democratic Control
dek: Democrats' majority path starts with holding Michigan and flipping North Carolina and Maine, then runs through Ohio, Texas, or Alaska.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: In 2026, Democrats start at a disadvantage: more than twenty of the thirty-five seats up for election are in states Trump carried by more than five points. Still, Trump's weak approval and Democratic overperformance in 2025 and early 2026 elections give the party a narrow Senate path.

In almost any Democratic majority scenario, North Carolina and Maine have to flip. The current forecast gives Maine about a 71% chance of electing a Democrat and North Carolina an over 88% chance of electing former Gov. Roy Cooper, making those two races the foundation of the Democratic path.

If Democrats flip North Carolina and Maine, Michigan becomes vital to hold. The state has a close three-way Democratic Primary, and the eventual nominee is likely to face Mike Rogers in a tough election. Despite what looks to be a tough election season for Michigan, the model currently gives Democrats roughly a 70% chance of holding the seat.

That would leave Democrats needing two more flips, most likely from Ohio, Texas, and Alaska. Ohio has the strongest chance out of the three to flip for Democrats, but the forecast shows it as close, with only a 55% of flipping. Texas and Alaska are harder, but either could flip if the national environment keeps moving toward Democrats.
